passage: To plot points on a Cartesian plane, we must always start from the origin, which is the intersection of the x-axis and y-axis at (0,0). When plotting the point (-2, 3), start at the origin and move 2 units to the left along the x-axis, then move 3 units up. It is vital to maintain equal spacing between numbers on your axes, regardless of where your data points fall, to ensure the graph is accurate. Once you have plotted several points for a linear relation, draw a straight line using a ruler that extends beyond the first and last points you marked. This line represents all possible solutions to the equation, not just the specific points you calculated. If you are tracking how a quantity like temperature changes over time, a line graph is the best choice, as it shows continuous trends. Avoid using pie charts for time-series data, as they are only meant to show parts of a whole at a single moment. Finally, remember that on a distance-time graph, a horizontal line indicates that the object is stationary, not moving at a constant speed.

items.q: Meena wants to plot the point (-2, 3). Starting at the origin, how should she move?
items.explain: The minus sign on -2 means move 2 units left from the origin, then 3 units up.

wrong.why: ignores the minus sign and moves right
thinks the first number tells how far up
moves the minus sign onto the wrong number

items.evidence: It is vital to maintain equal spacing between numbers on your axes, regardless of where your data points fall, to ensure the graph is accurate.
items.q: Asha's data values are 2, 5, 40 and 100. How should she space the numbers on her axis?
options: With equal gaps, whatever the data values
With gaps that follow where the data fall
With wider gaps for the bigger values
With gaps only around the data points
items.explain: Axis numbers must be equally spaced no matter where the data points fall, or the graph is inaccurate.

wrong.why: thinks spacing can follow uneven data
thinks bigger numbers need more room
thinks only the data values need marking

items.evidence: This line represents all possible solutions to the equation, not just the specific points you calculated.
items.q: Ravi drew a ruler line through the points he calculated for an equation. What do other points on that line show?
options: They are also solutions to the equation
They are drawing marks, not real solutions
They are solutions only between his marked points
They are solutions only where grid lines cross
items.explain: The line shows all possible solutions, not just the points Ravi calculated.

wrong.why: thinks only the calculated points are solutions
ignores that the line goes beyond the end points
thinks solutions must sit on whole-number grid points

items.evidence: Finally, remember that on a distance-time graph, a horizontal line indicates that the object is stationary, not moving at a constant speed.
items.q: A bus's distance-time graph stays horizontal from 2 pm to 3 pm. What was the bus doing then?
options: Driving on a flat, level road
items.explain: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means distance does not change, so the bus is stationary.

wrong.why: mixes up stationary with constant speed
thinks the line's shape is the shape of the road
thinks any line on the graph means movement
